newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. sees sharp cuts in European coal output, jobs.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sees sharp cuts in European coal output, jobs.

text.p: Further drastic cuts in coal production and employment are expected in eastern and western Europe over the next five to 10 years, as governments reduce or remove subsidies, a United Nations survey said.

Thereafter, both coal output and demand in the countries of the former Soviet Union are forecast to rise due to an expected economic recovery, while the downward trend is set to continue in western Europe due to rising energy efficiency and ecological control measures, the U.N. Economic Commission for Europe ((ECE) said.
In the meantime, the fall in coal output and consumption in both regions of Europe, including European areas of the former Soviet Union, has "temporarily halted" in 1996, the ECE said.

"In 1996, a temporary stabilisation of hard coal production is forecast for eastern as well as western Europe as a whole. However, further reductions in coal output are planned during the 1996-2005 period. In some countries, they could be drastic."

It cited France's decision to stop coal mining by 2005, proposals in Germany to cut output to 13 million tonnes by 2005 from the current 60 million, a restructuring plan in Poland and closure of 140 mines in Russia within seven years.

The ECE forecast that total hard coal output in eastern and western Europe would reach 534 million metric tonnes in 1996. (This figure does not include output in Kazahkstan, the second biggest producer among Soviet successor states).
Including Kazakhstan, European coal output is forecast to rise to 625.69 million tonnes this year, against 615.31 million in 1995.
In 1995, European hard coal output was 535 million tonnes, after falling by about 30 million from 1994.
Production represented 19 per cent of global output last year against 25 per cent in 1990.
The decline in European coal production, which is mainly mined underground and under difficult geological conditions, has accelerated since 1990, the ECE said.

"Since the underground coal in western Europe is produced at three times and more the price of coal in the world market, reducing production is seen by most countries as the only way out of the expensive coal industry," it said.
"In eastern Europe, too, costs and prices have become criteria in the restructuring plans for the coal industry."
